children: The Federal Reserve's Federal Open Market Committee is slated to vote this coming Wednesday on whether to raise, maintain, or lower interest rates.
We asked Seeking Alpha analysts
, and Michael Gray how divided they think the vote will be.

Leo Nelissen: Very. July was already a 9-3 vote, which was the most fractured decision since 2016, with Hammack, Kashkari, and Logan each dissenting in favor of a quarter point. Schmid and Musalem said afterward they would have joined had they been voting.

Since then, I think the situation has become even messier in both directions. For example, Waller asked his colleagues to look into disinflation. And while the lack of forward guidance means that this data won’t tell us much, I think the market could use that to price in more uncertainty (term premium).
That makes Warsh’s job important. If they aren’t careful, a breakout in longer-term rates could derail the market. I believe they will achieve the opposite, but the margin of error is thin.
(Leo Nelissen leads the SA investing group Main Street Alpha.)
Michael Kramer of Mott Capital Management: The CPI report on Friday made it difficult for the Fed not to raise rates at its September meeting.

If it skips this meeting, with the October meeting coming just days before the midterm elections, the next opportunity would be December, which is too long to wait. Most major central banks are in the process of raising rates, and the Fed is falling behind, which in the end will be bad for the dollar and put further pressure on inflation.
I don’t think the Fed will be divided. I think that if it chooses to hike, the decision will be unanimous.
(Michael Kramer leads the SA investing group Reading the Markets.)

Lawrence Fuller: I think we will see the same three voting members dissent at the upcoming meeting. I think Neil Kashkari, Beth Hammack, and Lorie Logan are likely to vote for a quarter-point rate increase. This division is likely to lead to a steepening of the yield curve with long-term Treasuries
weakening and yields rising to new highs on the year.
(Lawrence Fuller leads the SA investing group The Portfolio Architect.)
Michael Gray: This is going to be a true test of Warsh’s leadership.

Whatever the decision, it will be divided. Of the Fed governors who have spoken publicly in the past month, more have been in the rate hike camp. These include the three Fed presidents who voted for a rate hike in July, Fed Governor Lisa Cook, and Chairman Warsh.
That’s five votes.
In the hold camp, only New York Fed President John Williams and Governor Christopher Waller have spoken up, saying they’ll stay put unless inflation is hot.
The remaining committee members have remained quiet. All of them voted to hold in July, so the question is, has enough changed to have them shift their views?

The big concern from the July FOMC minutes was about inflation. Most expected that inflation would slow over the remainder of the year, but in part it was tied to easing of the Middle East conflict. That hasn’t happened.

Additionally, we’ve seen capital expenditures are rising, corporate profits are strong, and lending standards are on the historically easier side. As Warsh said, “I would be hard pressed to describe broad financial conditions as restrictive.”

In my view, this is enough to swing two to four of these members to the hike camp. The most obvious is Governor Jay Powell. Based on his history, the current situation of full employment and elevated inflation is one where he would support a hike. Plus, I believe he will side with Warsh. I also feel that there is enough evidence to sway at least a few of the other committee members to vote for a hike.
My best guess is 7-5 or 8-4 for a hike. Any larger majority will be a true testament to Warsh’s leadership skills.
Such a move, which I think is the right call, will prove Warsh’s, and the Fed’s independence.
There is only one person in the world who is publicly advocating for a rate cut. It’s a good thing he is not an FOMC member.

title: SA Asks: How divided will the FOMC vote be next week on raising rates?
